The risk of pollution by heavy metals, polychlorobiphenyls (PCBs), or dioxins is not different in the two modes of production
but it depends on exposure to atmospheric deposition. All outdoor productions, animal or vegetable, are most at risk. This is usually
the case for organic agriculture but also often for conventional agriculture, especially for the meat of grazing animals (Dervilly-Pinel
et al., 2017). Thus, milk from cows on pasture, whether organic or conventional, is less well protected than the milk from cows in
barn because the consumption of grass and soil may be an important vector of various pollutants. It is the same for eggs from hens
with outdoor run, often more contaminated than eggs from hens reared in cages.
For similar reasons, the risk of bacterial or viral contamination is greatest in outdoor production, from hydrotelluric sources (e.g.,
Clostridium botulinum) or contact with wildlife fauna (e.g., Campylobacter).
Microbial contamination of plants can be enhanced by the use of organic fertilizers compared to mineral fertilizers. Thus, the use
of manure, even composted, increases the risk of contamination of fruits and vegetables by Escherichia coli, Salmonella, or Listeria
monocytogenes. On the one hand, poultry manure from organic livestock is often contaminated with Campylobacter, which may
be an increased risk for eggs. However, according to several studies, these are only trends and, on the other hand, it appears that
